# Extending Programming Languages Through Schema-Driven Meta-Model Systems

## Overview

Modern software systems often require the ability to extend a programming language's capabilities to handle specialized data structures and validation logic without modifying the core language specification. This document describes a systematic approach for extending programming languages through the use of a strict meta-model, enabling developers to introduce custom keywords and behaviors while maintaining consistency and predictability across the extended language.

## Core Architecture and Interfaces

The system enables extending a programming language with a custom set of extensions by leveraging a strict meta-model that governs how new language features are defined, validated, and executed. This meta-model serves as the foundational contract that ensures all extensions adhere to consistent rules regarding structure, behavior, and integration with the underlying language runtime.

To facilitate this extensibility, a set of well-defined interfaces is provided that allows a schema to be synthesized programmatically. These interfaces abstract the complexity of schema creation, offering developers a structured pathway for defining the shape, constraints, and semantics of custom data objects. Building upon this schema synthesis capability, new syntax is introduced into the existing programming language, specifically designed to support the construction of schematized data objects. This syntactic extension allows developers to declare and instantiate complex data structures using natural, language-integrated constructs rather than relying on external configuration files or verbose boilerplate code.

## Schema Processing and Document Generation

At the heart of the system's translation capabilities lies a **schema processor module**, which is responsible for translating a schema representation into a corresponding set of new keywords. This module acts as a bridge between the abstract schema definition and the concrete language extensions that developers will use in their code. By converting schema specifications into keyword definitions, the schema processor effectively generates the vocabulary through which the extended language will operate.

Complementing the schema processor is a **document generator module**, which receives the keywords produced by the schema processor and generates output in a selected form. This modular separation of concerns—schema processing on one side and document generation on the other—allows the system to support multiple output formats and representations from a single, unified schema source. Developers can therefore target different serialization formats, documentation styles, or data representations simply by selecting the appropriate output configuration, without needing to redefine the underlying schema or keyword logic.

## Parsing and Execution Model

When code containing keyword extensions is parsed by the system, the parser constructs data structure nodes that represent keyword actions as functions. These nodes serve as an intermediate representation, capturing the semantic intent of each keyword in a form that can be systematically processed. The system then implements the corresponding function calls using the original meta-data associated with each keyword, ensuring that the behavior specified during schema synthesis is faithfully carried through to execution. This approach maintains a clean separation between the syntactic representation of keywords in source code and their underlying operational semantics, while preserving traceability back to the original schema definitions.

## Keyword Definition Structure

Each keyword definition within the system is composed of several essential components that govern its behavior throughout the language's execution lifecycle:

1. **Name**: A unique identifier that distinguishes the keyword within the extended language's vocabulary and allows it to be referenced within source code.

2. **Parse-Time Action**: A specified action that is executed at the moment the code is parsed. This action determines how the keyword is transformed or processed during the initial compilation or interpretation phase.

3. **Runtime Action**: A separate, specified action that is executed when the code is actually run. This action defines the operational behavior of the keyword during program execution.

By default, the parse-time action for a keyword is to **inject a function call** into the parsed representation of the code. This default behavior ensures that, even without custom configuration, every keyword produces a well-formed, callable construct within the resulting data structure. Correspondingly, the default runtime action is to **call that function**, thereby invoking the behavior associated with the keyword when the program reaches that point in execution.

This dual-action model—separating parse-time transformation from runtime execution—provides significant flexibility. Developers can override either the parse-time or runtime behavior independently, allowing for sophisticated customization scenarios such as compile-time validation, lazy evaluation, code generation, or deferred execution strategies, all while maintaining a consistent and predictable default behavior for straightforward use cases.

## Conclusion

This architecture provides a robust and extensible framework for augmenting programming languages with domain-specific capabilities. By combining a strict meta-model, dedicated schema and document processing modules, and a clearly defined keyword execution model, the system empowers developers to create rich, schematized language extensions that integrate seamlessly with existing codebases while preserving clarity, maintainability, and execution correctness.

# Extending Programming Languages with Custom Syntax: A Strict Meta-Model Approach

## Introduction

Modern software development increasingly demands flexibility in how programming languages handle domain-specific constructs. Rather than forcing developers to work within the rigid confines of a language's built-in syntax, there is growing interest in enabling controlled extensibility—allowing new syntactic forms to be introduced in a principled, predictable manner. This work addresses this challenge by presenting a strict meta-model approach for extending programming languages with custom syntax, providing a systematic framework that bridges the gap between schema definition, keyword processing, and executable code generation.

## The Core Challenge

Traditional approaches to language extension often suffer from ad-hoc implementations that are difficult to maintain, reason about, or integrate with existing toolchains. Developers seeking to introduce custom keywords or syntactic constructs typically face a tradeoff: either they build brittle, one-off parsers that are tightly coupled to specific use cases, or they attempt to modify the core language grammar, which is invasive and often impractical. What is needed is a principled architecture that allows new syntax to be defined declaratively, processed consistently, and executed predictably—all while maintaining a clear separation between the specification of *what* a keyword does and *how* it is integrated into the broader language ecosystem.

## The Strict Meta-Model Approach

To address this challenge, this work introduces a strict meta-model that serves as the foundational architecture for syntax extension. This meta-model is built around several interconnected components, each responsible for a distinct phase of the extension process.

### Interfaces for Schema Synthesis

At the heart of the approach are interfaces that synthesize schemas describing the structure and semantics of custom keywords. These interfaces provide a formal contract for how new syntactic elements should be represented, ensuring that schema definitions are consistent, composable, and machine-readable. By synthesizing schemas from interface definitions, the system establishes a clear and verifiable specification for each custom keyword before any parsing or execution takes place.

### Schema Processor

Once schemas are synthesized, a dedicated schema processor takes on the responsibility of translating these abstract representations into concrete new keywords that the language can recognize. This processor acts as a bridge between the declarative schema definitions and the operational vocabulary of the extended language, effectively compiling high-level schema specifications into actionable keyword definitions that downstream components can consume.

### Document Generator

Complementing the schema processor is a document generator, which produces structured output based on the processed keywords and their associated schemas. This component ensures that the results of schema processing are rendered into a coherent, structured format—one that can be consumed by other parts of the system or by external tools that need to understand the shape and behavior of the newly introduced syntax.

### Keyword Definitions: Parse-Time and Runtime Actions

A central feature of this meta-model is the dual nature of keyword definitions. Each keyword definition explicitly specifies two distinct types of actions:

1. **Parse-time actions**, which determine how the keyword is recognized, validated, and transformed during the parsing phase of code processing.
2. **Runtime actions**, which define the behavior that occurs when the parsed construct is actually executed.

This separation is crucial, as it allows keyword semantics to be cleanly divided between static analysis/transformation concerns and dynamic execution concerns, without conflating the two.

## Key Result: Seamless Integration Through Data Structure Nodes

The culmination of this architecture is a system in which parsed code generates data structure nodes that represent keyword actions as function calls. Critically, these function calls remain tied to their original meta-data, preserving the provenance and context of each keyword invocation throughout the processing pipeline.

This design yields several important benefits:

- **Default parse-time function injection**: The system automatically injects appropriate parse-time functions based on the keyword definitions, reducing the burden on developers to manually wire up parsing logic for every custom construct.

- **Runtime function execution**: Correspondingly, the runtime actions specified in keyword definitions are executed as part of normal program execution, ensuring that the custom syntax behaves as a first-class citizen within the broader language runtime.

- **Seamless integration of schematized data objects**: Perhaps most importantly, this architecture enables schematized data objects—objects whose structure and behavior are governed by the synthesized schemas—to be seamlessly integrated into existing programming languages. Developers can introduce custom syntax without disrupting the underlying language semantics or requiring extensive modifications to existing toolchains.

## Conclusion

By combining interface-driven schema synthesis, a dedicated schema processor, a document generator, and clearly defined parse-time/runtime keyword actions, this work presents a coherent and extensible framework for augmenting programming languages with custom syntax. The resulting system demonstrates that it is possible to introduce new syntactic constructs in a way that is both rigorous and practical—generating data structure nodes that faithfully represent keyword actions as function calls linked to their originating meta-data. This approach not only simplifies the process of language extension but also opens the door to more expressive, domain-specific programming paradigms that can be layered on top of existing languages without sacrificing consistency or maintainability.

# Systems, Embodiments, Syntax: On the Structure of Meaning

The relationship between systems, embodiments, and syntax reveals something fundamental about how meaning is constructed and communicated across domains—from language to computation to biological organization.

## Systems as Organizing Frameworks

A system is, at its core, a structured set of interrelated components that function according to defined principles. Systems provide the scaffolding within which individual elements gain significance through their relationships to one another. Whether we speak of linguistic systems, computational architectures, or ecological networks, the systemic view emphasizes that meaning rarely resides in isolated parts—it emerges from patterns of interaction, hierarchy, and constraint.

## Embodiments: From Abstract to Concrete

Embodiment refers to the process by which abstract principles or structures manifest in tangible, particular forms. An idea, a rule, or a system finds embodiment when it is instantiated—given a body, so to speak—in specific instances. In cognitive science, embodiment theory suggests that even abstract thought is grounded in bodily experience and sensorimotor interaction with the world. In software engineering, a design pattern is an abstract system that becomes embodied in actual code. In linguistics, grammatical rules find embodiment in the utterances speakers actually produce. Embodiment is thus the bridge between the general and the particular, the theoretical and the actual.

## Syntax: The Rules of Combination

Syntax governs how elements within a system combine to produce well-formed structures. While often associated narrowly with linguistic grammar, syntax in the broader sense applies to any domain where discrete units must be arranged according to rules to generate coherent wholes—musical notation, programming languages, even visual composition. Syntax is not merely decorative structure; it is generative, allowing finite sets of elements to produce infinite possible combinations, as Chomsky famously observed regarding natural language.

## The Interweaving of the Three

What makes this triad compelling is their interdependence. Syntax operates within systems—it is the internal logic that a system imposes on its constituent parts. Embodiments are the observable results when syntactic systems are applied to generate actual instances. Consider a sentence: the syntax of English (a system) permits certain word orders and structures; when a speaker utters an actual sentence, they embody that syntactic system in a concrete linguistic act.

This same pattern recurs in artificial intelligence, where formal systems (algorithms, models) rely on syntactic structures (code, logical rules) to produce embodiments (outputs, behaviors, decisions). It appears in architecture, where systems of structural engineering and syntax of spatial organization become embodied in physical buildings. It appears even in biology, where genetic systems, following molecular "syntax," become embodied in phenotypic organisms.

## Conclusion

Understanding the interplay between systems, embodiments, and syntax offers a powerful lens for analyzing how abstract order translates into concrete reality. Systems provide the framework, syntax provides the combinatorial logic, and embodiment provides the living instance—together forming a triadic structure that helps explain how meaning, form, and function arise across strikingly diverse fields of human knowledge and creation.

**System and Method for Extending Programming Languages Through Schema-Based Keyword Extensions Using a Meta-Model Architecture**

A system and method for extending existing programming languages with custom, schema-defined keywords without requiring modification of the underlying language compiler or interpreter. The system employs a meta-model architecture comprising: (1) a schema definition layer that allows developers to declaratively specify new keyword syntax, semantics, and validation constraints in a language-agnostic format; (2) a meta-model registry that stores keyword definitions as structured metadata, including type constraints, scope rules, and transformation logic; (3) a preprocessing and parsing engine that scans source code to identify registered keyword extensions embedded within standard language syntax; and (4) a code transformation module that translates recognized keyword extensions into valid, executable code in the target host language prior to compilation or execution.

The meta-model architecture enables dynamic registration, versioning, and composition of multiple independent keyword extensions, allowing extensions to be developed, distributed, and maintained separately from both the host language and one another. A validation subsystem cross-references keyword usage against the schema definitions to enforce type safety and semantic correctness at design time or compile time, generating diagnostic feedback prior to code generation. The system further supports extension namespacing to prevent keyword collisions and includes an integration layer for interfacing with existing integrated development environments (IDEs) to provide syntax highlighting, auto-completion, and error checking for the extended keywords.

This architecture allows software developers to introduce domain-specific language features—such as declarative data validation, workflow orchestration primitives, or domain-specific control structures—into general-purpose programming languages without forking the language specification or requiring end users to adopt a new toolchain, thereby improving developer productivity, code maintainability, and cross-project reusability of language extensions.

# Technical Disclosure: Schema-Driven Syntax Extension Framework for Existing Languages

## Abstract

This disclosure describes a system and method for extending the syntax of an existing programming or markup language through the coordinated operation of two cooperating modules: a **Schema Processor** and a **Document Generator**. The Schema Processor is responsible for defining, validating, and resolving new syntactic constructs against a formal schema, while the Document Generator consumes the schema-annotated intermediate representation to emit valid output in the target language's native syntax. This architecture enables incremental, non-invasive extension of established languages without modifying their core parsers, compilers, or toolchains.

---

## 1. Background and Problem Statement

Existing languages (e.g., configuration languages like YAML/JSON, markup languages like HTML/XML, or programming languages like Python/JavaScript) often lack native support for higher-level constructs that developers frequently need, such as:

- Reusable templates or macros
- Conditional inclusion/exclusion of blocks
- Cross-references and includes
- Typed annotations not supported by the base grammar
- Domain-specific shorthand notations

Traditionally, extending such languages requires either:
1. Forking the language's compiler/parser (high maintenance cost, fragmentation risk)
2. Building a completely separate DSL with its own toolchain (loses compatibility with existing tooling)
3. Using preprocessor macros with limited validation (error-prone, poor tooling support)

This disclosure proposes a two-stage pipeline that allows new syntax to be introduced as a **superset** of the existing language, validated against a schema, and then **compiled down** to fully valid, idiomatic output in the original language.

---

## 2. System Overview

The system comprises two primary modules:

```
┌─────────────────┐         ┌──────────────────┐         ┌────────────────────┐
│  Extended Input   │  --->  │  Schema Processor │  --->  │  Document Generator │  --->  Valid Output
│ (new syntax +     │        │  (validate/resolve│        │  (emit target       │        (native language)
│  base language)   │        │   /annotate AST)  │        │   language syntax)  │
└─────────────────┘         └──────────────────┘         └────────────────────┘
```

### 2.1 Schema Processor

The Schema Processor is responsible for:

1. **Schema Definition**: Maintaining a formal schema (e.g., JSON Schema, custom grammar definition, or type system) that describes:
   - New syntactic tokens/constructs and their allowed positions
   - Attributes/parameters each construct accepts
   - Type constraints and validation rules
   - Relationships between constructs (e.g., a `<template>` must be referenced before use)

2. **Parsing & Tokenization**: Extending the base language's parser via a **pluggable grammar layer** that recognizes new syntax markers (e.g., special prefixes, reserved namespaces, custom tags) while delegating all unrecognized syntax to the base language's existing parser.

3. **Validation**: Checking that new constructs conform to the schema — required fields present, types correct, references resolvable, no circular dependencies, etc.

4. **Semantic Resolution**: Resolving high-level constructs into a fully-specified **intermediate representation (IR)** — for example:
   - Expanding a `{% include %}` directive into the referenced content
   - Resolving a typed annotation into its expanded canonical form
   - Substituting macro parameters
   - Flattening conditional blocks based on evaluated conditions

5. **Error Reporting**: Producing structured diagnostics (line/column, construct name, expected vs. actual) that map back to the *original* extended source, not the intermediate form — critical for developer experience.

**Output of Schema Processor**: A validated, annotated AST/IR where every node is either (a) native to the base language, or (b) a resolved extension construct with all schema constraints satisfied.

### 2.2 Document Generator

The Document Generator is responsible for:

1. **IR Consumption**: Taking the annotated AST/IR produced by the Schema Processor as its sole input — it has no knowledge of the *original* extended syntax, only the resolved semantic structure.

2. **Target Serialization**: Emitting output strictly conforming to the grammar of the base/target language. This may include:
   - Pretty-printing rules (indentation, line length, quoting conventions)
   - Escaping/encoding required by the target language
   - Ordering constraints (e.g., imports before usage)

3. **Multi-Target Support**: Optionally supporting multiple output targets from the same IR (e.g., the same schema-validated source could generate YAML, JSON, or TOML), since the IR is decoupled from any single syntax.

4. **Round-Trip Metadata (optional)**: Embedding source maps or comments linking generated output back to the original extended source, to support debugging and error attribution in downstream tools.

**Output of Document Generator**: A fully valid document/program that can be consumed by the *existing, unmodified* toolchain for the base language.

---

## 3. Interaction Contract Between Modules

The two modules communicate through a well-defined **Intermediate Representation (IR)** contract, which decouples "what the syntax means" from "how it is rendered." This separation is the core novel aspect of the disclosure:

| Aspect | Schema Processor Owns | Document Generator Owns |
|---|---|---|
| New syntax recognition | ✅ | ❌ |
| Schema validation | ✅ | ❌ |
| Semantic resolution (macro expansion, includes, etc.) | ✅ | ❌ |
| Source-level error mapping | ✅ | ❌ |
| Target syntax formatting | ❌ | ✅ |
| Escaping/encoding rules | ❌ | ✅ |
| Multi-target emission | ❌ | ✅ |
| Output validity guarantees | ❌ | ✅ |

The IR itself is typically expressed as:
- A tree structure (AST) with typed nodes
- Each node tagged with schema-derived metadata (origin construct, validation status, source location)
- Extension-specific nodes fully "lowered" to base-language-equivalent nodes by the time they reach the Document Generator

This means the Document Generator **never needs to understand the new syntax** — it only needs to understand the resolved semantic primitives, which map 1:1 (or via known expansion rules) to base language constructs.

---

## 4. Example Walkthrough

Consider extending a YAML-like configuration language with a new `!include` construct and a typed enum annotation `!enum(RED, GREEN, BLUE)`.

**Extended Input:**
```yaml
color: !enum(RED, GREEN, BLUE) RED
settings: !include "common-settings.yaml"
```

**Schema Processor steps:**
1. Recognizes `!enum(...)` and `!include` as extension tokens via the pluggable grammar layer.
2. Validates `!enum` schema: value must be one of the declared set (`RED` ✅).
3. Validates `!include` schema: referenced file must exist and parse successfully.
4. Resolves `!include` by inlining the parsed content of `common-settings.yaml` into the AST.
5. Resolves `!enum` into a plain scalar node annotated with a validated-type marker (dropped in final output, or retained as a comment depending on config).
6. Produces annotated IR with no remaining extension tokens.

**Document Generator steps:**
1. Walks IR, sees only standard YAML node types (scalars, mappings, sequences).
2. Serializes to fully valid YAML:
```yaml
color: RED
settings:
  <inlined contents of common-settings.yaml>
```
3. Output is valid, unmodified YAML consumable by any standard YAML parser.

---

## 5. Extensibility Mechanism

New syntax is added to the system by:

1. **Registering a schema fragment** describing the new construct (name, allowed syntax pattern, parameters, validation rules).
2. **Registering a resolver function** with the Schema Processor that transforms a validated instance of the construct into base-language-equivalent IR nodes.
3. No changes are required to the Document Generator, *provided* the resolver only emits IR nodes the Generator already knows how to serialize.
4. If genuinely new *output* primitives are needed (rare), a corresponding serialization rule is added to the Document Generator's node-type dispatch table — but this is decoupled from any specific syntax and reusable across all extensions that resolve to that primitive.

This registration model allows third parties to define their own syntax extensions as plugins, each consisting of:
```
{
  schema: <JSON Schema or grammar fragment>,
  resolver: (node, context) => IRNode,
  diagnostics: <error message templates>
}
```

---

## 6. Advantages

1. **Non-invasive**: The base language's existing compiler/interpreter/toolchain remains completely unmodified — only preprocessing occurs.
2. **Composable**: Multiple independent syntax extensions can be layered, since each is resolved independently down to the shared IR.
3. **Separation of concerns**: Validation logic (Schema Processor) is fully decoupled from formatting/output logic (Document Generator), enabling independent evolution and testing of each.
4. **Multi-target reuse**: The same schema-validated IR can drive multiple Document Generators for different output syntaxes.
5. **Improved diagnostics**: Because the Schema Processor retains source-location metadata through resolution, error messages can reference the *original* extended syntax rather than generated output.
6. **Backward compatibility**: Documents using only base-language syntax pass through unchanged (Schema Processor performs no-op resolution, Document Generator effectively behaves as identity transform / pretty-printer).

---

## 7. Alternative Embodiments

- The Schema Processor and Document Generator could be merged into a single-pass streaming pipeline for performance-sensitive applications, provided the IR contract is preserved internally.
- The schema could be defined in the extended language itself (self-hosting), allowing schema definitions to be authored using the same extension mechanism.
- The IR could be serialized and cached, allowing the Document Generator to run independently/later (e.g., in a build step separate from validation), enabling separation of "author-time" and "build-time" concerns.
- Validation and resolution could be split into separate sub-modules within the Schema Processor to allow partial validation without full resolution (useful for IDE tooling/linting).

---

## 8. Claims-Style Summary (for reference)

1. A method for extending a base language's syntax comprising: receiving source text containing both base-language constructs and extension constructs; parsing said source text using a pluggable grammar layer; validating extension constructs against a registered schema; resolving validated extension constructs into an intermediate representation comprising only base-language-equivalent nodes; and generating output text conforming strictly to the base language's grammar from said intermediate representation.

2. The method of claim 1, wherein error diagnostics generated during validation reference source locations in the original, unresolved source text.

3. The method of claim 1, wherein the intermediate representation is consumable by multiple distinct document generators to produce output in multiple distinct target syntaxes.

4. The method of claim 1, wherein new extension constructs are added via a plugin registration mechanism requiring no modification to the document generator, provided the extension's resolver emits only previously-supported intermediate representation node types.

# Method for Custom Keyword Injection and Runtime Execution Binding

## FIELD OF THE INVENTION

The present disclosure relates generally to programming language processing systems, and more particularly to methods and systems for extending a base programming language's lexical and syntactic grammar through injection of custom keyword definitions at parse time, and for binding said custom keywords to executable function implementations resolved and invoked at runtime.

---

## BACKGROUND

Conventional programming language parsers operate against a fixed or statically defined grammar, wherein a finite set of reserved keywords is hard-coded into the lexer and parser components of a compiler or interpreter toolchain. Extension of language functionality typically requires modification of the underlying parser source code, recompilation of the toolchain, or reliance on preprocessor macro substitution—each of which presents drawbacks including maintenance burden, lack of runtime flexibility, and inability to support dynamic, user-defined, or plugin-supplied language constructs without redistribution of a modified compiler.

There exists a need in the art for a method whereby custom keywords may be registered, recognized during parsing, and bound to corresponding executable logic without requiring modification of the core parsing engine, thereby enabling extensible, modular, and dynamically configurable language grammars.

---

## SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

In accordance with one or more embodiments, a method is provided for injecting one or more custom keyword definitions into a parsing system at parse time, and for executing one or more corresponding functions associated with said custom keywords at runtime. The method generally comprises:

1. Receiving, by a keyword registration subsystem, one or more custom keyword definitions, each definition comprising at least a token identifier, a syntactic pattern, and a reference to an executable handler function;
2. Injecting said custom keyword definitions into an extensible grammar table accessible to a lexer/tokenizer and a parser during a parse-time phase;
3. Tokenizing source code input using the extended grammar table such that occurrences of the custom keyword are recognized as distinct lexical tokens rather than being treated as generic identifiers;
4. Parsing said tokens into an abstract syntax tree (AST), wherein nodes corresponding to custom keywords are annotated with metadata linking said nodes to their respective registered handler functions;
5. Traversing the AST at runtime and, upon encountering an annotated custom-keyword node, resolving and invoking the corresponding handler function, optionally passing contextual arguments derived from sibling or child nodes in the AST.

This architecture permits dynamic extension of a programming language's surface syntax without modification of the core parser or lexer source code, and further permits late binding of behavior to newly introduced syntactic constructs.

- **FIG. 3** — Flowchart illustrating the runtime resolution and invocation of handler functions.
- **FIG. 4** — Example abstract syntax tree annotated with custom keyword metadata.

---

## DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION

### 1. System Overview

Referring to FIG. 1, the disclosed system comprises the following functional components, which may be implemented in software, firmware, hardware, or any combination thereof, and which may be distributed across one or more computing devices comprising at least one processor and at least one non-transitory computer-readable storage medium storing instructions executable by said processor:

- **(a) Keyword Registry Module (110)** — a data structure, such as a hash table, trie, or associative array, configured to store custom keyword definitions, each definition comprising:
  - a unique token identifier (e.g., a string literal such as `"whenever"`, `"unless_all"`, or an arbitrary user-defined symbol);
  - an associated syntactic pattern or grammar production rule specifying how the keyword may be combined with other tokens;
  - a reference (e.g., function pointer, closure, callback identifier, or symbolic name) to a handler function to be invoked at runtime.

- **(b) Grammar Injection Module (120)** — a component configured to merge or splice the custom keyword definitions from the Keyword Registry Module (110) into an existing base grammar definition, producing an extended grammar definition, without requiring modification of the source code implementing the base grammar.

- **(c) Lexer/Tokenizer Module (130)** — configured to consume source code text and the extended grammar definition, and to produce a token stream in which custom keywords are represented as distinct token types (as opposed to being classified generically as identifiers or literals).

- **(d) Parser Module (140)** — configured to consume the token stream and construct an abstract syntax tree (AST), wherein nodes corresponding to recognized custom keywords are tagged with metadata references linking each such node to the corresponding handler function reference stored in the Keyword Registry Module (110).

- **(e) Runtime Execution Engine (150)** — configured to traverse the AST at execution time, detect annotated custom-keyword nodes, resolve the associated handler function reference, marshal any required arguments from the AST context, and invoke the handler function, optionally capturing a return value for further use in program execution.

---

### 2. Parse-Time Keyword Injection Process

Referring to FIG. 2, in one embodiment, the method of injecting custom keywords at parse time comprises the following steps:

**Step 210 — Registration:** A caller (e.g., a plugin, module, library, or end-user configuration file) supplies a custom keyword definition to the Keyword Registry Module (110). The definition may be supplied via, without limitation: a configuration file (e.g., JSON, YAML, XML), a programmatic API call, a decorator or annotation within source code, or a domain-specific registration language.

**Step 220 — Validation:** The Grammar Injection Module (120) validates the proposed keyword definition against the existing base grammar to detect conflicts (e.g., collision with an existing reserved keyword) and, in the event of a conflict, either rejects the registration, raises a warning, or applies a disambiguation strategy such as context-sensitive scoping (e.g., the keyword is only active within a designated code block, namespace, or file scope).

**Step 230 — Grammar Extension:** Upon successful validation, the Grammar Injection Module (120) generates an extended grammar definition by adding one or more production rules corresponding to the custom keyword, said production rules specifying the token's expected position, arity, and permissible surrounding syntax (e.g., prefix keyword, infix operator, block-introducing keyword, or annotation-style decorator).

**Step 240 — Lexer/Parser Reconfiguration:** The extended grammar definition is supplied to the Lexer/Tokenizer Module (130) and Parser Module (140), which reconfigure their internal state (e.g., regenerating a finite state automaton, updating a parsing table such as an LALR or LL(k) table, or updating a recursive-descent dispatch table) to recognize the newly introduced keyword token.

**Step 250 — Source Parsing:** Source code is tokenized and parsed using the reconfigured lexer and parser, producing an AST in which nodes corresponding to the custom keyword are annotated with a metadata tag referencing the associated handler function.

In alternative embodiments, said grammar extension and reconfiguration may occur incrementally and repeatedly during a single parsing session, permitting keywords to be registered and recognized in a streaming or incremental parsing context, such as within a read-eval-print loop (REPL) or a live-editing development environment.

---

### 3. Runtime Function Resolution and Execution Process

Referring to FIG. 3, the method of executing functions corresponding to custom keywords at runtime comprises:

**Step 310 — AST Traversal:** The Runtime Execution Engine (150) traverses the AST produced by the Parser Module (140), using any suitable traversal strategy (e.g., depth-first, breadth-first, or a visitor-pattern-based traversal).

**Step 320 — Node Inspection:** For each node encountered, the Runtime Execution Engine (150) inspects the node for the presence of custom-keyword metadata previously attached during the parse-time process.

**Step 330 — Handler Resolution:** Upon detecting such metadata, the Runtime Execution Engine (150) resolves the referenced handler function, which resolution may comprise a direct function pointer dereference, a symbol table lookup, a dynamic dispatch through a registry keyed by keyword identifier, or a late-binding lookup permitting the handler implementation to be modified after parse time but before execution.

**Step 340 — Argument Marshaling:** The Runtime Execution Engine (150) extracts contextual data from the AST node's children, siblings, or enclosing scope (e.g., literal values, variable references, nested expressions) and marshals said data into an argument list, argument object, or parameter binding suitable for consumption by the handler function.

**Step 350 — Function Invocation:** The Runtime Execution Engine (150) invokes the resolved handler function with the marshaled arguments, within the current execution context (e.g., current stack frame, variable scope, or execution sandbox).

**Step 360 — Result Integration:** Any value returned by the invoked handler function is optionally captured and integrated into the ongoing program execution, e.g., bound to a variable, used as an operand in an enclosing expression, or used to control subsequent execution flow (e.g., branching, looping, or early termination).

---

### 4. Alternative Embodiments

In accordance with further embodiments:

- **(a)** The custom keyword definitions may support parameterization, wherein the syntactic pattern includes placeholder tokens for operands, and the handler function receives said operands as typed arguments.

- **(b)** The custom keyword may be scoped to a namespace, module, or file, such that identical keyword tokens may be bound to different handler functions in different scopes without collision.

- **(c)** The Keyword Registry Module (110) may support versioning and hot-reloading, such that handler function bindings may be updated, replaced, or removed during a running process without requiring re-parsing of previously parsed source code, provided that the Runtime Execution Engine (150) performs late resolution of the handler reference at each invocation rather than caching a resolved reference at parse time.

- **(d)** The grammar injection may be implemented via a plugin architecture, wherein third-party modules register keyword definitions through a public API exposed by the Grammar Injection Module (120), thereby enabling extensibility without modification of the host language's core distribution.

- **(e)** The handler function may itself be defined in a different programming language than the source code being parsed, and invocation may occur via a foreign function interface (FFI), inter-process communication (IPC) channel, or remote procedure call (RPC), such that custom keywords in a source language may trigger execution of native, compiled, or remotely hosted logic.

- **(f)** Conflict resolution between multiple registered keyword definitions bearing the same token identifier may be resolved via a priority ranking, a most-recently-registered rule, an explicit override declaration, or a compile-time error requiring explicit disambiguation by the developer.

---

# PATENT CLAIMS

## Claim 1
A computer-implemented method for extending a programming language through custom keyword definitions, the method comprising:

receiving, by a language processing system, a keyword definition specifying:
(a) a keyword identifier for recognition during source code parsing;
(b) a parse-time action defining syntactic transformation or validation logic to be executed when the keyword identifier is encountered by a parser;
(c) a runtime action defining executable behavior to be invoked when code containing the keyword is executed;

registering the keyword definition within a keyword registry accessible to both a parsing subsystem and a runtime execution subsystem;

during a parsing phase, detecting an occurrence of the keyword identifier within source code being parsed;

responsive to detecting the occurrence, invoking the parse-time action associated with the keyword identifier, wherein the parse-time action generates or modifies an abstract syntax tree (AST) node corresponding to the keyword occurrence, the AST node comprising a reference to the runtime action;

during a subsequent execution phase, traversing the AST and, upon encountering the AST node comprising the reference to the runtime action, invoking the runtime action to produce an execution result.

## Claim 2
The method of claim 1, wherein the parse-time action comprises at least one of:
- validating syntactic arguments following the keyword identifier against a defined grammar;
- transforming the keyword occurrence and associated syntax into one or more equivalent AST nodes representing existing language constructs;
- emitting a parse-time diagnostic or error when the syntactic arguments do not conform to the defined grammar.

## Claim 3
The method of claim 1, wherein the runtime action comprises executable code that is bound to the AST node at parse time and is invoked with a runtime execution context comprising variable bindings, a call stack reference, and an evaluation environment.

## Claim 4
The method of claim 1, further comprising storing, in the keyword registry, for each registered keyword definition, an association among the keyword identifier, the parse-time action, the runtime action, and a precedence or scope indicator determining applicability of the keyword definition within a given lexical or module scope.

## Claim 5
The method of claim 4, further comprising resolving conflicts between two or more keyword definitions sharing an identical keyword identifier by applying the precedence or scope indicator to select an applicable keyword definition for a given source code location.

## Claim 6
The method of claim 1, wherein registering the keyword definition comprises receiving the keyword definition from a plugin or extension module loaded into the language processing system independently of a core language implementation.

## Claim 7
The method of claim 1, further comprising:

determining, by the parsing subsystem, whether the parse-time action requires additional syntactic input beyond the keyword identifier; and

responsive to determining that additional syntactic input is required, invoking a sub-parser specified by the keyword definition to consume the additional syntactic input and produce a corresponding sub-tree for inclusion in the AST node.

## Claim 8
The method of claim 1, wherein invoking the runtime action comprises passing to the runtime action one or more argument values derived from evaluation of child nodes of the AST node prior to invocation.

## Claim 9
The method of claim 1, further comprising caching a compiled or partially evaluated form of the runtime action following a first invocation, and reusing the cached form for subsequent invocations of the AST node during execution.

## Claim 10
The method of claim 1, wherein the keyword definition further specifies a compile-time-only flag, and further comprising, responsive to the compile-time-only flag being set, omitting generation of the reference to the runtime action within the AST node such that the keyword produces no runtime behavior.

## Claim 11
A system for extending a programming language through custom keyword definitions, comprising:

one or more processors;

a memory storing instructions that, when executed by the one or more processors, cause the system to:

maintain a keyword registry storing a plurality of keyword definitions, each keyword definition comprising a keyword identifier, a parse-time action, and a runtime action;

parse source code using a parser configured to consult the keyword registry, detect keyword identifiers within the source code, and invoke corresponding parse-time actions to generate AST nodes referencing corresponding runtime actions;

execute the source code using an execution engine configured to traverse the AST and invoke the runtime actions referenced by the AST nodes to produce execution results.

## Claim 12
The system of claim 11, wherein the parser comprises an extensible tokenizer configured to recognize the keyword identifier as a distinct token type based on the keyword registry, independent of a set of reserved keywords defined by a base grammar of the programming language.

## Claim 13
The system of claim 11, wherein the instructions further cause the system to expose an application programming interface (API) enabling a third-party module to register a new keyword definition with the keyword registry at a time prior to parsing of source code that utilizes the new keyword definition.

## Claim 14
The system of claim 11, wherein the execution engine is configured to invoke the runtime action within a sandboxed execution context that restricts access to a subset of system resources based on a permission attribute specified in the keyword definition.

## Claim 15
A non-transitory computer-readable medium storing instructions that, when executed by one or more processors, cause the one or more processors to perform operations comprising:

receiving a keyword definition comprising a keyword identifier, a parse-time action, and a runtime action, and storing the keyword definition in a keyword registry;

parsing input source code, including detecting the keyword identifier and invoking the parse-time action to produce an abstract syntax tree node associated with the runtime action; and

executing the abstract syntax tree, including invoking the runtime action associated with the abstract syntax tree node to generate a result of executing the input source code.

## Claim 16
The non-transitory computer-readable medium of claim 15, wherein the operations further comprise dynamically unregistering a previously registered keyword definition from the keyword registry, and, responsive to the unregistering, causing the parser to treat subsequent occurrences of the corresponding keyword identifier as an ordinary identifier token rather than as a keyword.

---

# SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

The present invention relates to systems and methods for extending a programming language by allowing developers to define custom keywords, each associated with both a **parse-time action** and a **runtime action**. Unlike conventional language extension mechanisms that require modification of a compiler or interpreter's core source code to introduce new syntactic constructs, embodiments of the present invention provide a **keyword registry** that stores keyword definitions independently of the core language implementation, enabling third-party modules or plugins to introduce new language features without altering the underlying parser or execution engine.

Each keyword definition comprises three principal components: (1) a keyword identifier used to recognize the keyword during lexical analysis and parsing; (2) a parse-time action, which is invoked when the parser encounters the keyword identifier and which is responsible for validating associated syntax, optionally invoking sub-parsers to consume further tokens, and generating or transforming a corresponding node in an abstract syntax tree (AST); and (3) a runtime action, which is referenced by the generated AST node and is invoked during execution of the program to produce a computational result.

By decoupling the parse-time behavior from the runtime behavior, while linking them through a shared AST node reference, the invention enables a single keyword definition to govern both how the keyword's associated syntax is validated and transformed at compile time, and how the corresponding functionality is executed at runtime. This architecture supports dynamic registration and unregistration of keyword definitions, scope- and precedence-based conflict resolution among competing definitions, caching of compiled runtime actions for performance optimization, and restriction of runtime actions to sandboxed execution contexts for security purposes.

Various embodiments further provide for compile-time-only keyword definitions that produce no runtime behavior, extensible tokenizers capable of recognizing registered keywords independent of a language's base reserved-word set, and application programming interfaces through which external plugins may contribute new keyword definitions prior to the parsing of source code that depends upon them. The disclosed system thereby provides a flexible, modular, and secure mechanism for extending programming languages with new syntactic and semantic constructs.

# SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

The present disclosure relates generally to systems and methods for automated document generation, and more particularly to a software architecture that translates schema representations into a domain-specific set of language keywords for generating structured documents.

In accordance with one aspect of the present disclosure, a computer-implemented system is provided that receives one or more schema representations defining structural, semantic, and relational properties of data intended for inclusion in a structured document. The system comprises a schema analysis module configured to parse the schema representation and extract a plurality of schema elements, including but not limited to field names, data types, nested object relationships, cardinality constraints, and validation rules.

In accordance with another aspect, a keyword generation engine is disclosed, operatively coupled to the schema analysis module, configured to map the extracted schema elements to a corresponding set of newly defined language keywords belonging to a target markup or programming language. The keyword generation engine may employ a translation table, rule-based mapping logic, or a trained machine learning model to associate schema constructs with semantically appropriate keyword equivalents, such that the generated keywords preserve the structural intent and data relationships expressed in the original schema representation.

In some embodiments, the system further comprises a document synthesis module configured to receive the generated language keywords and to assemble a structured document therefrom, wherein the structured document may include, without limitation, extensible markup language (XML) documents, JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) documents, configuration files, template files, or other machine-readable or human-readable document formats.

In accordance with a further aspect, the architecture includes a validation module configured to verify that the structured document generated from the translated keywords conforms to one or more predetermined formatting rules, schema constraints, or syntactic requirements associated with the target language, thereby ensuring consistency and correctness of the output document.

In some embodiments, the system may further include a feedback loop wherein discrepancies identified during validation are communicated back to the keyword generation engine to iteratively refine the mapping logic, thereby improving translation accuracy over successive operations.

Additional aspects of the present disclosure include methods for performing the above-described translation and generation processes, as well as non-transitory computer-readable media storing instructions that, when executed by one or more processors, cause the one or more processors to perform the disclosed methods.

It is to be understood that both the foregoing general description and the following detailed description are exemplary and explanatory only and are not intended to be limiting of the invention as claimed. Other systems, methods, features, and advantages of the present disclosure will be, or will become, apparent to one of ordinary skill in the art upon examination of the following drawings and detailed description.
